idiom_name: thread_local storage specifier plus confinement by ownership
implementation_notes: C++11's `thread_local` storage specifier makes the hand-rolled per-thread registry unnecessary for long-lived per-thread state: namespace-scope and static block-scope variables get one instance per thread, initialized on first odr-use in that thread and destroyed at thread exit. Ordinary objects need no mechanism at all - a worker's stack locals, `std::thread`/`std::jthread`-owned state or a private arena are confined by construction as long as no reference escapes; assert thread affinity (compare `std::this_thread::get_id()`) where review alone is not enough. The classic structures (a thread-affinity wrapper, a key-backed registry) remain justified when objects must be looked up dynamically per thread or when the toolchain is pre-C++11.
pitfalls: thread_local objects are destroyed at thread exit in reverse construction order; a destructor touching another thread_local or a static during shutdown can see it already destroyed.

In shared libraries, TLS models and dlopen can create additional instances per load (each with lazy per-thread initialization), and foreign helper threads may touch TLS before the module initialized it.
A thread_local slot defined in a header can silently multiply per translation unit; use an inline variable (C++17) or a single defining TU for one logical slot.

variants.name: pthread keys / Boost.Thread thread_specific_ptr (pre-C++11)
variants.implementation_notes: Before C++11, and for dynamically looked-up per-thread pointers in portable code, thread-specific data is built on the platform key API: pthread_key_create once (commonly via pthread_once) plus pthread_setspecific/pthread_getspecific per access, with a destructor run at thread exit; Boost.Thread's `thread_specific_ptr<T>` wraps the same mechanism portably, deleting the stored object or invoking a custom cleanup routine on reset and thread exit. This form costs a lookup per access, stores `void*` (no type checking) and needs explicit thread-exit cleanup, whereas thread_local needs none; it is still the right choice on C++03 toolchains or when slots must be created at runtime. Boost.Thread documents that cleanup only happens for threads it created unless `boost::on_thread_exit()` is called manually.
pitfalls: Destructor functions run at thread exit in unspecified order relative to other keys and to C++ thread_local objects (glibc destroys thread_locals first), so cleanup must not depend on other per-thread data.

PTHREAD_KEYS_MAX is small (as low as 128 usable in practice); keys must be created once per logical slot, and boost::thread_specific_ptr relies on cleanup callbacks that leak on natively created threads unless manually triggered.
The stored void* is untyped and unreferenced by the runtime: after a thread exits, a cached pointer to its slot is a dangling read with no compiler help.
